The post Endowment is the missing pillar of university finance appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Gordon Cox, Director at Philanthropy Company and former Director of Advancement at the University of Bath and Development Fellow at University College, Oxford.

For decades, debates about university funding in the United Kingdom have centred on public grants, tuition fees and research income. Yet one of the most important sources of long-term financial resilience remains largely underdeveloped outside a few UK institutions: the university endowment. This is not simply a fundraising issue; it is a question of strategy, governance and policy.

The central argument of my report is straightforward: universities that systematically build and manage endowments are better positioned to withstand financial shocks, invest in new priorities and support future generations. Endowments are not a substitute for public funding, but they can complement existing income streams and support a more balanced, sustainable funding model.

Endowment internationally – a strong, underused tradition in the UK

The contrast between the UK and international competitors is striking. The Council for Advancement and Support in Education (CASE) data show that outside Oxford and Cambridge, UK universities collectively hold around £5 billion in endowment assets and generate approximately £150 million annually, representing just 0.3 per cent of sector income. Moreover, only about 10 per cent of philanthropic income goes to endowments, compared with nearly 29 per cent in the United States.

This gap is not due to a lack of tradition, as Britain has one of the world’s richest histories of endowed education. Oxford, Cambridge and the Wolfson Foundation all demonstrate the transformative potential of long-term capital when supported by effective governance and disciplined investment. The problem is that much of the wider sector has not translated this historical legacy into a modern strategy.

Building strong endowments has been a hallmark of US institutions and has served as a foundation for many of these institution’s transformational ideas, (including named professorships and tuition reducing or eliminating scholarship programs). The case has been made why all institutions, especially those throughout the UK, should refocus their efforts on building strong endowments to support their future success.

Joshua R. Newton, Senior Vice President, Advancement and Alumni Engagement, Chair of CASE50.

How universities can build sustainable endowment income

The report identifies three recurring features of successful endowment systems: professional management, sufficient scale and close alignment between investment and fundraising. When these conditions are in place, institutions tend to achieve stronger returns, inspire greater donor confidence, and generate higher levels of long-term support.

There is a crying need for a centralised, well-run university endowment investment. There needs to be more of a long-term approach, and universities should be thinking along a time horizon, but many do not.

Paul Ramsbottom, CEO, Wolfson

Size drives performance and the opportunity for growth

Scale appears particularly important, with international and domestic evidence consistently showing that larger endowments generate stronger returns because they can access specialist investment expertise, diversify more effectively and manage costs more efficiently. Smaller and fragmented funds struggle to achieve the same outcomes. Oxbridge’s experience, along with the Wolfson Foundation and several international case studies, suggests that pooled investment structures can offer a practical route to overcoming this challenge.

Small endowments don’t have the scale … you’re not going to get the level of professional management … or access to the best managers.

Andrew Reid, Director of Finance, University of Cambridge, 2001-2018.

In the UK context, the independent colleges of the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge have pooled endowment assets over recent decades, providing a powerful example of how shared investment and administrative services can generate significant impact, reduce costs, and improve efficiency. A similar approach, with universities pooling endowments to manage them collectively, as they already do through shared pension arrangements, could be adopted more widely across the higher education sector. By achieving greater scale, institutions could strengthen investment performance, improve diversification and reduce management costs. (Universities UK (UUK), Transformation and Efficiency).

The implications are significant, and the report’s modelling with CASE and Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) data suggests that relatively modest improvements in investment performance and fundraising could substantially increase endowments’ contribution to university finances over time. Under current assumptions, endowment income remains a marginal contributor to sector revenues. However, higher investment returns and directing a greater share of philanthropic income into endowments could generate materially larger, more sustainable income streams. In many cases, such as at the National University of Singapore and to a lesser extent, all Singapore universities, endowments have grown remarkably quickly.

The power of compounding and aligning fundraising and investment strategies

The modelling is illustrative rather than predictive, but it highlights compounding’s power over long periods. One modest scenario suggests that the non-Oxbridge endowment base could grow from approximately £5 billion to around £38 billion over 20 years if fundraising and investment practices align and improve.

Learning from global experience and history

This report draws extensively on global case studies and evidence from across the higher education sector, examining historical trends and emerging practice in the stewardship, investment, and fundraising of university endowments. The analysis draws on sector insights from organisations including BUFDG, the Russell Group, and CASE, and is complemented by two virtual panel discussions featuring senior leaders from four continents.

Endowment has long been an important part of Newcastle University’s story and of the wider university sector. Yet in recent generations across the country, its potential has sometimes been overlooked. Strong leadership can play a crucial role in developing endowment as a source of long-term, diversified income that benefits future generations of students, researchers and university leaders. At Newcastle, we have recently embraced many of the changes highlighted in this report, and I hope others across will find it a valuable investment of their time and support.

Professor Chris Day, Vice-Chancellor and President, Newcastle University

The panels below bring together vice-chancellors, university executives, investment professionals, fundraising leaders, and philanthropy advisers, offering a broad international perspective on the opportunities and challenges of endowment development. Their collective experience highlights both the barriers to building endowments and the practical strategies institutions can adopt to enhance long-term financial sustainability and philanthropic support.

Key themes & recommendations

Professionalised investment models

Importance of scale

Blended funding models

Fundraising capability and culture

Donor expectations: flexibility, impact and trust

Governance as a key success factor

Influence of the external environment

Balancing restriction and flexibility

Leadership and moments of change

Redefining endowment purpose and time horizon

Communication, collaboration and sector constraints

Lessons from the Yale investment model

This is an important report raising awareness of how universities could increase the impact they can achieve through endowment funds. While progressing the proposals would be complex and require a long-term outlook, we would encourage the sector to take seriously the opportunity to increase funding to university endowments. Key to achieving success will be to deepen stakeholder understanding of what endowments are and what they are not. CASE looks forward to learning how this report is received more widely and to participating in future discussions.

Sue Cunningham, President and CEO of the Council for Advancement and Support of Education (CASE)

Panel 1: Leaders in higher education

Drawing on experience in university leadership, public policy, philanthropy, and investment management, the panel offers practical insights into the opportunities and challenges of building long-term institutional strength through endowments. Together, these perspectives help contextualise the report’s findings within the realities of contemporary higher education leadership and strategic decision-making.

Gordon Cox and Nick Hillman facilitate a discussion featuring Matt Cox, Director of Investment at University College London; Sir Ivor Crewe, former Master of University College, Oxford and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Essex; Carole Souter CBE, former CEO of the Heritage Lottery Fund and Master of St Cross College, Oxford; and Ian White CBE, former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Bath and Master of Jesus College, Cambridge. The discussion examines how university leaders approach endowment governance, investment strategy and stewardship.

https://youtu.be/NXSwo9WbHuw

Panel 2: Leaders in philanthropy and advancement

In this discussion, three leading advancement professionals from Asia, Australia and the United States explore with Gordon Cox international perspectives on endowment fundraising, investment governance and donor engagement.

Featuring Edi Fung, Vice President for Advancement at the National University of Singapore, Rosalind Ogilvie, Director of Advancement at the University of Sydney, and Josh Newton, Senior Vice President for Advancement and Alumni Engagement at Emory University, the panel draws on extensive experience of leading major fundraising campaigns, building philanthropic partnerships and strengthening long-term institutional support. Together, they share insights into global trends, emerging opportunities and the lessons universities can learn from successful approaches to philanthropy and endowment development.

https://youtu.be/fXJxabsApqI

Together, these discussions offered practical perspectives on how universities across jurisdictions approach endowment growth, governance and stewardship. The contributions complement the report’s evidence and international case studies and place the findings within the realities of contemporary higher education leadership and fundraising practice.

title: Labor Watch: Harvard Workers Strike Again, CSU Makes Deals
summary:
Labor Watch: Harvard Workers Strike Again, CSU Makes Deals Emma Whitford Thu, 11/05/2026 - 03:00 AM Also in October, Department of Education workers in Chicago filed an OSHA complaint about unsafe working conditions and Tufts University sued its non-tenure-track faculty union to stop the reinstatement of a professor fired for violating the sexual misconduct policy. Byline(s) Emma Whitford Labor Watch: Harvard Workers Strike Again, CSU Makes Deals
Emma Whitford Thu, 11/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

Also in October, Department of Education workers in Chicago filed an OSHA complaint about unsafe working conditions and Tufts University sued its non-tenure-track faculty union to stop the reinstatement of a professor fired for violating the sexual misconduct policy.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
As its faculty union prepares to strike, California State University announced contract agreements with five other labor unions over the past several weeks. Most recently, the 14,500-strong California State University Employees Union—which represents health care, administrative, technical, operational and student support staff in the system—reached a tentative agreement that includes a salary-step framework with predetermined raises based on performance and years of service, plus a $3,575 bonus in December.

“This tentative agreement reflects the CSU’s commitment to reaching fair and responsible agreements with our labor partners while recognizing the important contributions of CSUEU-represented employees across the university system,” CSU Chancellor Mildred García said in a news release. “We look forward to the ratification process and to continuing our work with CSUEU on behalf of the employees who help our universities serve California’s students and communities.”

Four other shops—United Auto Workers Local 4123, which represents academic student workers; Academic Professionals of California, which represents academic advisers and career counselors; the International Union of Operating Engineers Local 39, which represents engineers, maintenance personnel and technical workers; and the Statewide University Police Association—also inked deals with CSU. All of the new contracts include a similar step system for salaries, and they are awaiting ratification votes, according to the news release.

But not all CSU labor unions are satisfied. About a year into bargaining, the California Faculty Association opened a strike vote Oct. 26. Faculty members and university officials remain at odds over academic freedom protections, salaries and workload. Members have until Nov. 19 to decide whether to authorize a strike. CSU’s skilled trade workers union—Teamsters Local 2010—also filed two new unfair labor practice charges against the system last month, accusing leaders of bad-faith negotiations and interfering with union actions, according to a union news release.

“CSU cannot refuse to bargain fairly with our members and then interfere with workers’ rights when they stand up and fight back,” Jason Rabinowitz, secretary-treasurer of the union, said in the release. “Our members have fought too hard for the wages and respect they deserve to continue being disrespected by CSU. These charges send a clear message that we will hold CSU accountable and keep fighting for fair wage increases and a strong successor contract.”

Strikes were hot in October. Several other shops, including unions representing Harvard University academic workers and Massachusetts Institute of Technology graduate student workers, approved strikes. Meanwhile, the City Colleges of Chicago narrowly averted a planned strike. Also in this edition of Inside Higher Ed’s Labor Watch, Tufts University sued its union over the reinstatement of a teaching professor, and U.S. Department of Education workers in Chicago raised concerns about their working conditions.

STRIKE ALERT: Members of the Harvard Graduate Student Union–United Auto Workers have been on strike since Oct. 27, when the 4,000-some graduate student workers walked off the job following a stalemate over wages, protections for international workers and grievance processes for harassment and discrimination. It is HGSU-UAW’s second strike this year; previously, the union struck for 40 days in the spring.

“Harvard has refused to offer meaningful proposals or schedule additional, on-the-record bargaining sessions. We are ready to bargain at any time,” Denish Jaswal, president of HGSU-UAW, said in a statement. “We would rather be teaching and doing research. But we need a contract we can live and work under. We are prepared to stay on strike until Harvard moves.”

Meanwhile, the MIT graduate student workers union set a Nov. 12 strike deadline. The union remains deadlocked with MIT officials over wages and international worker protections. If the two parties do not reach a tentative agreement with university officials before the deadline, the 3,000-plus members will walk off the job.

“We are asking for perfectly reasonable measures in this contract. Wages that keep up with the rising cost of living, protections for international workers in a precarious political climate, and for MIT to take back proposals they have put forward targeting the strength of our union,” Baltasar Dinis, a graduate worker and bargaining committee member, said in a news release. “We sit across from MIT’s corporate lawyers who respond to these issues with presentations about how they need to keep growing the endowment. Nearly seven months of bargaining have shown us that the MIT administration is completely out of touch with the experiences of the graduate workers who make MIT what it is.”

STRIKE AVERTED: The City Colleges of Chicago’s faculty and professional staff union averted a strike last month, reaching a deal hours before the deadline. The contract agreement includes annual cost-of-living raises, expanded parental leave, health insurance protections and safeguards against artificial intelligence, WTTW reported.

“I am proud of our negotiating teams, of our members who were prepared to strike, and of this contract,” Cook County College Teachers Union Local 1600 President Tony Johnston said in a statement to WTTW.

TRYST AT TUFTS: Tufts University is suing its non-tenure-track faculty union, asking the court to vacate an arbitral decision to reinstate a professor who was fired for engaging in sexual activity with his girlfriend in his campus office, The Tufts Daily reported.

A student doing homework in the next room overheard Theodore Simpson, a teaching professor, “engaged in various sexual acts which were both audible and explicit,” according to the complaint. The student recorded the sounds and immediately reported it to Tufts’s Office of Equal Opportunity. When Tufts officials investigated, Simpson lied and said he had been watching a sexually explicit movie, Betty Blue.

After he was fired, the Service Employees International Union Local 509 brought the case to arbitration, where an independent arbitrator ultimately ruled that Simpson must be reinstated with a written reprimand and argued his conduct, which did not include penetrative sex, was not severe enough to warrant termination.

Tufts officials say their sexual misconduct policy doesn’t distinguish between types of sexual activity and that they have an obligation to remedy harassment and, therefore, dismiss Simpson. The case was filed in Massachusetts district court.

DON’T DRINK THAT: The union representing 2,000 Department of Education employees filed a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration last month about unsafe working conditions at the agency’s regional office in Chicago. Employees say they have documented multiple instances of Legionella bacteria, which can cause severe pneumonia, in the water since 2023. Last month, an employee reported that an elevator “shook forcefully and appeared to descend at an increasingly rapid and uncontrolled speed,” according to a news release.

“The public servants in this building deal with unclean drinking water, faulty elevators, unsafe electrical work and an insect infestation,” American Federation of Government Employees Local 252 President Rachel Gittleman said in a news release. “It is unacceptable to expect professionals to work in an unsafe environment where their health and safety are at risk.”

title: The 90-Credit Degree Deserves a Name of Its Own
summary:
The 90-Credit Degree Deserves a Name of Its Own Elizabeth Redden Thu, 11/05/2026 - 03:00 AM We owe it to students, graduate schools and employers to clearly distinguish 90-credit degrees from the traditional bachelor’s. Byline(s) John G. Harris The 90-Credit Degree Deserves a Name of Its Own
Elizabeth Redden Thu, 11/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

We owe it to students, graduate schools and employers to clearly distinguish 90-credit degrees from the traditional bachelor’s.

Byline(s)
John G. Harris
full_text:
The basic structure of American undergraduate degrees has remained roughly constant for decades. A bachelor’s degree requires about 120 semester credits and four years of study, while an associate degree requires about 60 semester credits and two years of study. The rising popularity of 90-credit degrees creates a third category of undergraduate degrees requiring about three years of full-time study.

My institution, the Missouri University of Science and Technology, currently does not offer any 90-credit degrees. But we are considering whether to offer them in the future, and our discussions about these new programs have focused my thinking on what we should call them. Leaders have a responsibility to establish a distinct name for the emerging 90-credit degree rather than treating it as a qualified or diminished version of the bachelor’s degree. If it is to offer a true alternative to what already exists, the new degree needs a single, straightforward label that clearly distinguishes it.

I am in favor of 90-credit degrees for multiple reasons. First, there is a compelling economic case for students and their families: Completing a degree in three years could save an entire year of tuition and related college costs and allow graduates to start earning a salary one year sooner. Second, some professions seem well suited to employ graduates of three-year, highly applied degree programs that go deeper than a typical associate degree but don’t necessarily require a full bachelor’s-level curriculum.

Three-year degrees are gaining increasing attention (from proponents and opponents alike) and many colleges have already created them: A RAND national inventory identified 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs announced by U.S. colleges as of May of this year. Some of these new programs bear the same titles of bachelor of arts or bachelor of science as conventional 120-credit programs. This raises issues of intelligibility for employers and graduate schools. Cutting a degree from 120 credit hours to 90 is significant, but an employer reviewing two résumés may not realize the distinction in degree requirements if both degrees share the same title. Graduate schools will face similar issues when deciding whether a 90-credit and a 120-credit B.S. both satisfy their admissions requirements. Students are the most at risk as they decide between 90-credit and 120-credit programs with the same name.

To its credit, the Commission on Colleges and Universities, formerly known as the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges, requires universities to use a modifier to distinguish the 90-credit degree from a traditional 120-credit bachelor’s degree. A number of universities throughout the country add a modifier to the name of the bachelor’s degree such as “accelerated,” “applied,” “abridged” or “reduced-hour.” But this does not solve the problem. Qualifiers can easily disappear as credentials move from catalogs to résumés and job applications. Furthermore, some of these modifiers already have established meanings. For example, an accelerated bachelor’s degree traditionally refers to completing a traditional 120-credit bachelor’s degree in less than four years, through heavy semester course loads and summer classes. A 90-credit degree is a different model, and using the same label for both blurs the distinction between them.

I suggest the adoption of the term “practitioner degree” for the 90-credit degree. “Practitioner” is a simple English word that is already used in some professional hierarchies. For example, the Federation for Informatics Professionals uses levels progressing from associate practitioner to practitioner, followed by senior, advanced and leading practitioner. The practitioner-degree label can serve as a starting point for discussion—another name may prove more suitable across the full range of undergraduate disciplines. The specific name matters less than establishing a separate third category of degree.

A simple framework might look like this:

60-plus credits: associate degree, approximately two years

90-plus credits: practitioner degree, approximately three years

120-plus credits: bachelor’s degree, approximately four years

This overall framework would give students and employers clearer and more meaningful choices. A student seeking rapid entry into the workforce might conclude that a 90-credit degree offers the right combination of education, cost and time to employment. A student planning to attend graduate or professional school might choose the traditional 120-credit bachelor’s degree. Students may change their minds and switch between degrees as they progress. An employer might find a 90-credit graduate ideally prepared for one position while another position may be a better match for a 120-credit graduate. Students, families, employers and graduate programs should make these determinations. Our responsibility in higher education should be to make the distinctions clear enough for them to make informed decisions.

The new degrees should not be seen as lesser versions of existing degrees. They have their own purpose and are formed differently from bachelor’s degrees. If we call a 90-credit program a bachelor’s degree, the natural tendency will be to begin with an existing 120-credit bachelor’s and determine which 30 credits to eliminate. General education courses and electives then become obvious targets for reduction. That approach risks turning the new degrees into watered-down versions of existing four-year programs. The Commission on Colleges and Universities has explicitly, and wisely, recommended that institutions “design an intentional curriculum framework rather than simply removing electives” from 120-credit degrees.

We should also look at the opportunity from the other direction. Instead of reducing existing bachelor’s degrees, institutions could build upward from strong two-year associate degrees. A 60-credit associate degree could serve as the foundation for an additional year of advanced coursework, producing a distinct three-year degree. This approach creates something new rather than simply removing pieces from something old. It also gives both four-year universities and two-year community colleges more freedom to rethink what a three-year undergraduate education should accomplish and how it meets the needs of the student populations they serve.

Many universities will resist giving up the term “bachelor’s degree” because they fear a newly named degree will be less attractive to prospective students. But this concern proves the point. If students see a 90-credit degree differently because it has a different name, keeping the bachelor’s label would obscure the differences in academic requirements. Institutions should compete for students by demonstrating the value of their programs, not by falsely using a familiar degree name to conceal distinctions.

A second objection is that many job ads explicitly require a bachelor’s degree, and graduates with a practitioner degree would not appear to qualify. However, if employers conclude that a 90-credit degree meets their needs, they will say so in their job postings. Universities should not make that decision for them.

A third, related objection is that a new name will take time to be accepted and students could face uncertainty during the transition, especially on the job market. That concern is real, but it is not a reason to avoid clarity and transparency. We already have an accepted structure where roughly two years of study leads to an associate degree and roughly four years leads to a bachelor’s degree. A three-year degree lies somewhere between the two. As such degrees become more popular, students with practitioner degrees could be encouraged to apply for jobs requiring bachelor’s degrees and let employers decide.

Higher education leaders and institutional accreditors must establish a standard name for these 90-credit degrees now, before the bachelor’s label, with or without one of the many competing modifiers, becomes entrenched. We should welcome these new degrees by defining their value clearly and not relying on confusing language that could mislead students, employers and graduate schools.

title: Post-secondary students across Ontario walk out of classrooms to protest OSAP changes, tuition hike
summary: University and college students across Ontario are protesting rising tuition fees and the province's cuts to the Ontario Student Assistance Program in a provincewide walkout Thursday.
full_text:
University and college students across Ontario are protesting rising tuition fees and the province's changes to the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) in a walkout Thursday.

"Students have had enough of being asked to pay more, borrow more and accept less," Cyrielle Ngeleka, chair of the Canadian Federation of Students (CFS) Ontario, said at Queen's Park Thursday.

"We have witnessed hundreds of programs cut, student services stretched and the cost of education pushed further onto the backs of students and their families."

The walkouts are part of CFS Ontario's "Hands Off Our Education!" campaign, with protests sprouting up on several campuses across Ontario, including York University, the University of Guelph, Trent University and University of Windsor.

"There has been very real impacts to students based on these OSAP cuts," said University of Guelph student and president of the school's student union Emilie Dudgeon.

"There are students who can't afford to pay their rent and live in the city. There are students that are questioning whether or not they're going to be able to afford to come back next semester."

The protest comes after the province lifted a seven-year tuition freeze earlier in the year, which allowed universities and colleges to increase fees by up to two per cent each year over the next three years.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government has also been under fire for the larger part of the year after announcing changes to OSAP in February, citing "unsustainable" costs.

Changes to the student assistance program meant non-repayable grants were reduced from a maximum of 85 per cent to 25 per cent, while the percentage of funds given as loans increased. Many students have said scaled-back OSAP grants will saddle them with high debt loads amid economic uncertainty.

The province has defended the changes, highlighting its $6.4-billion investment in Ontario colleges and universities, which will be rolled out over the next four years.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said the funding will help institutions provide competitive programs, high standards of education and be “resilient” to growing demands in the future.

"The previous OSAP framework was no longer sustainable," said Quinn's press secretary, Bianca Giacoboni.

"Our government is ensuring Ontario students have access to an affordable world-class education that will launch them into good paying jobs and careers for many years to come.”

Education is a right: student

At York University, students and supporters gathered at 9 a.m. with signs reading "OSAP weaves futures, not baskets," (in response to a previous comment from Ford) and "Education should not be a debt sentence."

Symone Lennon, president of the York Federation of Students, shouted "Tax on students" into a microphone as the crowd replied "Vote it down!"

"Every single student deserves to be here," Lennon told CBC Toronto. "The message is simple. It's not only 'fund OSAP,' it is simply 'fund our education as students' because we have a right to be here and it is not a privilege."

Lennon says one of her friends was forced to take time off from attending university because of changes to OSAP, and she herself is nervous about her future in a competitive job market.

"The future is looking quite bleak right now, for not only just me, but a number of students," she said.

Recent York University graduate Sam Jean told CBC Toronto that he had heard some high schoolers were deferring post-secondary education because of changes to OSAP.

"It's just completely pulled the rug out from a whole generation of students," said Jean. "A lot of students acutely feel like we don't have a future."

Jax Carter, a first-year student at the Ontario College of Art and Design, says the increasing cost of education is part of a larger problem.

"We're meeting a lot of students today who are very angry," said Carter. "Toronto is one of the most expensive cities to live in. Not only can we not afford rent, they expect us to pay more for our education."

Opposition parties support protesting students

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said in a news release she stands with students protesting Ford's changes to OSAP.

"Doug Ford has spent this year attacking students," said Stiles. "We called on [Ford] to come up with a plan to provide immediate relief to students who need financial assistance. He and his government refused.

"They've made it clear that they have no interest in helping Ontario students.... Now, the Premier has no choice but to hear their voices."

Ontario Greens Leader Mike Schreiner expressed the party's support for university students in a statement Thursday.

"Young people are struggling to get by in an economy stacked against them. It’s never been harder to get a job and a record number of youth are being forced to choose between a roof and food," he said.

"Now more than ever, we should be working to shrink student debt and remove barriers for young people — not sticking them with tens of thousands of dollars of debt."

Schreiner called on the Ford government to reverse changes to OSAP, remove interest on student loans and unlock frozen funds so low and middle-income students can access non-repayable grants.

In addition to changes to student assistance to college and universities in Ontario, the provincial government has recently frozen OSAP funding for private career colleges after an audit found "serious concerns."

title: Can democracy be taught? Brazil is about to find out
summary: Brazil has just made civic education compulsory in schools. Whether it takes hold will depend less on the law than on what happens in the classroom.
full_text:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

Brazil’s experience offers lessons for other democracies, including Europe, that are turning to education to strengthen democratic resilience.

Knowing how institutions work is not enough: democracy is learned through experience as much as via content.

Civic education mandates often fail between the law and the classroom. Teachers, time and democratic school life decide whether they take hold.

In Brazil’s presidential run-off on October 25, President Lula turned the result around against the odds by winning a fourth term with 51.77% of the valid votes. It was the first time since Brazil’s return to democracy that the runner-up in the first round went on to win.

First-round abstention reached 21.08 %, the highest rate in a presidential election since 1998. It fell to 19.22% in the run-off, but more than 30 million eligible voters still stayed away.

This is no one-off: abstention has crept up since 2006, when it stood at 16.75%. Experts blame disenchantment after decades of scandals and two presidential impeachments, voters registered in towns they have left, and fines up to R$3.51, less than one euro, for those who neither vote nor justify their absence. In a country where voting is compulsory for most adults, seeing it as a right, rather than merely a duty, will require a deeper cultural shift.

That shift begins long before election day, through civic education : learning not only how democracy works, but how to question, act and influence public life by tackling concrete problems in their communities.

Yet civic education received little attention in the campaign. In his platform, Lula proposed a national digital literacy policy to combat disinformation. The policy would teach people of all ages, especially older people, to navigate the internet critically, but the programme says little about schools. Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, pledged schools that teach students “how to think, not what to think”, free from partisan indoctrination, and more civic-military schools.

Beyond electoral promises, what is Brazil’s long-term vision for preparing citizens to take part in democracy?

A promise on paper

Brazil’s 1988 Federal Constitution already states that education must prepare people for the exercise of citizenship. The 1996 National Education Guidelines and Bases Law (LDB) made this one of the core aims of basic education, and the National Common Core Curriculum (BNCC) includes citizenship among the skills every student should develop.

Yet the gaps are large. The 2022 International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS) found significant gaps in Brazilian students’ civic knowledge. According to the OECD’s 2024 Truth Quest Survey, Brazilians had the lowest ability among 21 countries to distinguish between true and false or misleading online content, with an accuracy rate of 54%, compared to an average of 60%.

In September 2025, the executive branch responded: a ministerial ordinance created the Brazilian Ministry of Education’s Programme for Citizenship and Sustainability Education. Joining is voluntary, yet by July 2026 all but one of Brazil’s 26 states and 57% of its municipalities had signed up.

Its competency matrix sets out 46 skills, from pre-school to the end of secondary school, in three strands :

fundamental rights and environmental citizenship

the democratic ecosystem and its defence

citizenship in practice.

Pupils should learn, for example, to recognise democratic breakdowns and authoritarian proposals in Brazil’s history, to understand what the Supreme Court and the leaders of both houses of Congress do, to tell free speech from hate speech, and to take part in their school’s democratic bodies, such as student councils.

Networks that join must appoint a coordinator and draw up a local plan, and teachers can take online courses on the ministry’s platform. The programme’s own guide acknowledges “significant gaps” in citizenship education in Brazil, and promises a national plan to monitor implementation and learning outcomes.

In July 2026, more than a decade after the original bill was introduced, a new law amended the LDB to make civic education a compulsory curricular component.

It is not the first time. In 1969, the military junta made moral and civic education compulsory at every level, alongside a secondary-school subject called Brazilian Social and Political Organisation (OSPB). Among its stated aims was “the cult of the homeland, its symbols, traditions and institutions”. After the return to democracy, a 1993 law abolished both and folded their content into the humanities. Civic education is therefore, not new to Brazil.

The challenge is to understand what each curriculum really sets out to teach.

The new law has an unusual cross-party history. It was signed under Lula’s government, but originated in a bill by federal deputy Renata Abreu, leader of Podemos, a party that formally backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the run-off.

In a deeply polarised country, could civic education become a rare point of common ground?

Its reach will also depend on how the law and the programme fit together, since one is compulsory and the other is voluntary. Ideally, each feeds the other: the law gives the 43% of municipalities still outside the programme in July a reason to join, and the programme gives schools the means to comply. Together, they could take civic education to every school; apart, many schools will face a new duty without the means to meet it.

From law to the classroom

The law makes civic education compulsory, but not necessarily as a standalone subject. It could be woven into existing classes, such as history, geography and Portuguese, or taught through interdisciplinary projects. Given the autonomy of Brazil’s education systems, some states could also make it a separate subject.

Much remains to be defined. The law does not specify teaching hours, grade levels, teacher qualifications or materials. Its incorporation into the National Common Core Curriculum still requires approval by the National Education Council and ratification by the education minister. Only then will states, municipalities and schools adapt their curricula.

In October, the electoral court and the education ministry agreed to work together on regulation, teaching materials and school election simulations. Learning by doing has a track record: since 2004, the Chamber of Deputies’ Youth Parliament has brought 78 secondary school students to Brasília for each edition, to debate and vote on bills as if they were deputies. But such programmes reach few pupils, and institutional commitment is only a first step.

Nor is the new law consensual. Associations of philosophy and social science teachers asked for a veto, fearing it would weaken philosophy and sociology, and the Escola sem Partido movement warned of ideological indoctrination. Though raised from different angles, both concerns point to the same condition for success: teachers trained not only in content, but in a professional ethic above party lines, so that students learn to form their own views rather than adopt someone else’s.

Brazilians even have an expression for laws that never take hold: “Leis que não pegam.” This gap is precisely why Politize !, the non-partisan civic education institute I co-founded in 2015, has run its Active Citizenship School programme for over eight years. In Brazilian public schools alone, more than 19,000 teachers have used its training and materials to reach around 288,000 students. In 2026, this work earned Politize! the European Union’s Human Rights Award in Brazil.

For the new law to take hold, civic education must be cross-curricular but with clear owners, interdisciplinary but not diluted, and non-partisan but not depoliticised. It will need teacher training, suitable materials, curricular time, coordination and monitoring.

Could this law become the opportunity to bring civic education to scale across Brazil?

When democracies turn to the classroom

Brazil would not be the first country to turn to the classroom when its political order is under strain. In such moments, civic education is less an education policy than an attempt to rebuild a shared democratic project.

In 1952, a West Germany rebuilding after Nazism and war created a federal agency to consolidate and spread democratic and European ideas among Germans, today’s Federal Agency for Civic Education. In 1976, a meeting of educators from across the political spectrum gave rise to the Beutelsbach Consensus : teachers must not indoctrinate, must present contested issues as contested, and must enable students to take part in democracy. Fifty years on, it remains the standard in German classrooms, and a useful reference for Brazil’s own fears of indoctrination.

Latin America offers closer parallels. In Chile, after a wave of corruption scandals, a 2016 law required every state-recognised school to adopt a citizenship education plan and paved the way for a compulsory subject, Citizenship Education, in the final two years of secondary school, which was introduced in 2020. In Colombia, a 2014 law passed during peace talks with the FARC guerrillas made a course on the culture of peace compulsory in every school and a 2015 decree required it to be assessed in the national school-leaving exam.

Other countries have focused on participation. In Argentina, a 2013 law requires education authorities to recognise and support student councils in secondary schools. In Mexico, the electoral authority, INE, gives children and teenagers the opportunity to vote on issues that affect them: more than 10 million people aged 3 to 17 took part in 2024.

Across Latin America, civic education often stops at declarations. A 2020 UNESCO review of primary-school curricula in 19 countries in the region (Brazil’s included) found that citizenship features in all of them, but that such concepts appear more often in statements of principle than in the content teachers use to plan lessons.

Europe shows that a place in the curriculum is only half the battle. Italy, for instance, made civic education compulsory in 2019 as a cross-curricular subject of at least 33 hours a year, shared among each class’ teachers and taught since 2020.

Across Europe, the weak link has been teacher preparation. When the EU’s Eurydice network reviewed 42 education systems in 2017, 17 had no central rules or recommendations on preparing future teachers for citizenship education, and only 13 of the 36 systems that taught it across subjects defined what all future secondary teachers should master.

A new Eurydice report, due in December, will show what has changed and give Brazil and its neighbours a benchmark. In the end, teachers decide whether civic education takes hold, and they can only do so if education systems prepare and support them.

A lesson from the run-off

Brazil’s run-off showed what is at stake. Citing transport failures and floods, Supreme Court justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours nationwide, after both campaigns had requested extensions in some areas. Flávio Bolsonaro called the decision unacceptable, refused to concede and said he would seek to annul the election. Whether the decision was right is for institutions to judge.

Within days, after Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered him to surrender his passports in a money-laundering investigation, Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the United States. His allies called it political exile from judicial persecution. Critics, Lula among them, replied that “those with nothing to hide have nothing to fear”, and some suggested he was getting ahead of January, when his Senate term ends, and with it the special legal standing it grants. Each side tells a ready-made story.

When politics works more like a clash of tribes, or a form of entertainment, than a shared civic space, no school subject can protect citizens on its own.

What civic education can offer is a shared grammar for such decisive moments on the political agenda: separating facts from narratives, accepting results, and contesting electoral proceedings and practices through evidence, transparency and the courts.

Lula’s new term will be the first to implement the law that seeks to promote civic education. Making it work will require treating civic education as state policy, not government policy.

Brazil already obliges its citizens to vote; the harder task is preparing them to vote well and to take part in democracy between elections. If the law succeeds, the country will have shown the many democracies now turning to the classroom that democracy can be taught and, above all, practised.

title: US midterm elections: what could change for international education?
summary:
The Democrats’ win in the US midterm elections could have implications for international students studying in the US, amid Trump’s tightening of restrictions on study and post-graduate opportunities.

The post US midterm elections: what could change for international education? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, securing majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives. They also flipped key Senate seats in traditionally Republican states, such as Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932.

This sweeping wave of blue across the US comes at an important time for international students studying in the country, as the Trump administration continues to restrict the opportunities available to them.

Reacting to the win, Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said the results “underscored that voters are paying attention to fairness and common sense talk and proposals.”

“The next Congress will have an important opportunity to examine the cumulative effects of visa delays and denials, travel restrictions, immigration enforcement impacting campuses, and limits on practical training,” she added.

The Democratic victory means that the Trump administration will face greater opposition in Congress, making it harder to pass legislation without Democratic support. They will also be able to block or delay presidential appointments requiring Senate confirmation, and could force the White House to negotiate over legislation.

Most recently on October 7, The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released a proposed rule which would charge US universities $70,000 for each international student they recommend for Optional Practical Training (OPT). Institutions would have to pay a further $30,000 per year for extensions of a student’s initial OPT.

If implemented, the proposed fees could also make it harder for universities to sustain the additional costs of supporting international students.

In August, DHS announced that Curricular Practical Training (CPT), the program allowing international students to take internships and work placements during their studies, should only be granted where it is a degree requirement.

This prompted the cancellation of thousands of internships for international students, according to organisations challenging the move, with Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Penn among the institutions to review or tighten their rules.

The Presidents’ Alliance said it would like to see “forward-looking solutions” that “provide more predictability and certainty for students, institutions, and employers” to build a system that “welcomes international students and scholars.”

One student, who preferred to remain anonymous, told The PIE News that they feel “relief” but are still “cautious” about what the future may hold for international students in the US.

“The policies that hurt us most were executive orders, not legislation. A Democratic Congress can apply pressure, but it cannot undo those orders on day one…Around campus I sense cautious optimism, but also exhaustion, people have been through too much uncertainty to get excited over one election night.”

They say “the damage to the US brand as a study destination has already happened” and that students who left this year “will not return” because of the election result.

The midterm elections, which take place halfway through a president’s four-year term, mark a crucial point in a presidency, as Americans vote for members of Congress, the body responsible for creating and passing federal laws.

These laws apply nationwide and must be passed by both chambers of Congress before being approved by the president. The president can sign or veto a bill, but Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate.

The results therefore determine how easy it will be for the current president to carry out their legislative plans, although many immigration policies can still be pursued through executive action.

Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, said the results would not change the organisation’s “unwavering” mission to champion international education, advocate for students and scholars, defend the value of global engagement, and stand firmly for the dignity, opportunity and belonging of all.

“International education matters. It is a bridge that connects us to each other and the world, reminding us that our future is strengthened by being part of the world, not apart from it,” she added.

title: Professional Ecosystems: Harmonious Alignment for Faculty Service

The post Professional Ecosystems: Harmonious Alignment for Faculty Service appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
As faculty members, we often discuss the pressures of the classroom and research; yet, the demands of service remain largely overlooked. Junior faculty, in particular, can feel compelled to join committees, spearhead university initiatives, lead student organizations, and foster community partnerships. This burden is even heavier for those from marginalized or underrepresented backgrounds, who often find themselves conforming to molds not built for them. Whether joining prestigious but unfulfilling committees or executing a senior faculty’s community project, these performative tasks often lead to burnout and isolation. Ultimately, these systemic pressures drive talented faculty to leave their universities-or higher education all together.

Cultivating Professional Ecosystems

In their book, Good Work: When Excellence and Ethics Meet, Howard Gardner, Mihaly Csikszentmhalyi, and William Damon pose a question that sparked a transformative journey for me: What can people do when conditions threaten a harmonious alignment? Reflecting on this prompted me to interrogate my own burnout and reimagine how to nurture my love for the academic community around me. From this experience, I developed the Professional Ecosystem Framework. This framework is designed to guide faculty in cultivating their own service focus by emphasizing belonging, reclaiming, and healing. It consists of three strata – a term chosen over “components” or “elements” to evoke the geological and ecological layers that inherently support one another. The three strata that intertwine to create the Professional Ecosystem Framework are:

Living Arbors: Unearthing Radical Belonging with Ancestral Roots – This stratum of the framework moves beyond the idea of a network and encourages faculty to see themselves as a canopy. Within this stratum, we create shade for others while ensuring their own roots have the space to drink.

Un-Grafted Seeds: Nurturing Self in Sovereign Soil – In horticulture, grafting forces a vine onto foreign roots. However, this stratum of the framework is about embracing your ancestral soil, nurturing your lived experiences, and showcasing your unique strengths.

Reciprocal Harvests: Envisioning Praxis as Medicine – Work that feeds the community must also feed the worker. This stratum redefines productivity as a cycle of communal empowerment and personal healing.

Theoretical Foundations

The roots of the Professional Ecosystem Framework are planted within two theoretical perspectives. The first theoretical perspective shaping the framework is Chicana feminism. This theoretical perspective guides the framework’s emphasis on the collective, spiritual, and familial aspects of service (Anzaldúa, 1987; Garcia, 2014). Within this also exists a heightened awareness that our experiences are often rooted in resistance that is gendered, racial, and class-based (Bernal, 1998).

The second theoretical perspective nurturing the framework is the Relational Indigenous Leadership Philosophy (RILP) developed by Hardison-Stevens (2022). This philosophy has tribal ways of knowing affiliated with the Omushkeg Cree-Metis, Ojibway, Cowlitz, and Stilacoom peoples. The RILP first acknowledges that our sensory awareness guides us through spaces not created for us. Rather than focusing on authoritative hierarchies or Eurocentric views of knowledge, RILP emphasizes self-advocacy, community well-being, and stewardship.

Developing Your Own Professional Ecosystem

Stratum 1: Living Arbors

My grandmother once spoke to me of human towers or castells, which come from a Catalonian tradition where humans stand on the shoulders of others in order to create a tower that stands over a hundred feet tall. She reminded me that the most important part of the tower is not the victorious individual at the top; rather, it is the people who are at the bottom. Starting the journey to build my own ecosystem required a re-evaluation of my human tower. My colleagues often looked upward towards those at the top with institutional power, but I knew I had to return to my roots and pay attention to those at the foundation of my tower. I had shamefully neglected my relationships with aunties, cousins, or fiends who lacked formal university educations. In healing those connections, I discovered that their insights are as essential to my academic journey as any institutional guidance or alliances.

As you reflect on your human tower, consider reflecting on the following: Who is woven into your ecosystem and who has been overlooked? As a faculty member, you know that having a department chair or dean in your corner is powerful. However, when you tap into the ancestral roots of your background and invite individuals from your past into your current academic life, new growth begins. This new growth creates a canopy of protection not only for yourself but also for others who come from similar backgrounds.

Stratum 2: Un-Grafted Seeds

The next stratum of the framework was more challenging for me. I was caught up in the comparison game and compared my service and leadership to colleagues around me. I finally engaged in introspection and identified unique skills I bring to the table. For example, I had been a single mother, and I had lived on government assistance. These aspects of my life had cultivated unique skills many of my colleagues did not have.

As you reflect on your uniqueness, consider reflecting on the following: What lived experiences have cultivated strengths, and how might these strengths serve you in academia? If you are struggling to answer some of these questions, considering exploring the community cultural wealth model (Yosso & Burciaga, 2016). Her model considers different aspects of capital that are often overlooked in Eurocentric spaces. As you explore this second stratum of the framework, remind yourself that the goal is not to graft onto a foreign root but to allow your unique lived experiences nurture authentic strengths.

Stratum 3: Reciprocal Harvests

Reflecting on the first two strata solidified my decision to change my service focus. I began to envision my own praxis as medicine for myself and others. While the other service areas at my university were worthwhile, they did not resonate with me. I sought out initiatives that promoted healing myself and others, leading me to establishing a campus clothing closet for students, assisting parenting students, and developing a mentorship program for Latinas.

As you cultivate this stratum of the framework, consider asking yourself- How can I advocate for students in ways I wish someone had advocated for me, and how can I turn that into initiatives that nurture my academic community? As mentioned earlier, work that feeds the community must also feed the worker. This last stratum of the framework allows you to still be productive but within communal spaces of care.

Conclusion

We must move from a culture that consumes its members to one that cultivates them. Like the strata of the forest or the earth on which we stand, having a professional ecosystem creates an intertwining layer of support. Rather than engaging in the competitive nature of higher education, which can often make you feel like you are being eaten alive, we can shift the culture to one of curious cultivation. By modeling our own professional ecosystem, we do more than just survive the pressures of higher education, we become a part of the transformation for others.

Aimée Myers, PhD, is an Associate Professor of Literacy and Language at Texas Woman’s University. She also serves as the Associate Dean of Academic Affairs in the College of Professional Education. Her teaching specialization focuses on culturally responsive-sustaining practices. In her research, she works to utilize social constructivist, decolonized approaches with underserved populations. Her current studies include visual testimonios with immigrant and refugee students and community cultural wealth with graduate students from underrepresented backgrounds. She is the coordinator of the COPE Clothing Closet, the founder of the Latinx Juntos Mentorship program, and the facilitator for the Urban Education Microcredential.

title: Dialogue, Trust, and Learning in the Age of AI: Why Students Belong at the Table
summary:
On a Tuesday morning last semester, students in my Writing II class engaged in debate. After the topic of AI and college classes came up, a spokesperson for one group, a young woman, spoke up from the back of the room, beginning with “I’m in college for a reason.” She said, “Sure, I could ask […]

The post Dialogue, Trust, and Learning in the Age of AI: Why Students Belong at the Table appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
On a Tuesday morning last semester, students in my Writing II class engaged in debate. After the topic of AI and college classes came up, a spokesperson for one group, a young woman, spoke up from the back of the room, beginning with “I’m in college for a reason.” She said, “Sure, I could ask ChatGPT to summarize an article for me, but how does that build my analytical skills?”

She continued; we listened (and I found myself internally nodding yes to each point she made). In those moments, I felt myself relax, the opposite of the usual apprehension I feel when AI is being touted by PD-pitchers or debated among teachers. I thought – This is what has been missing: the student voice.

Our AI-infused world has ushered in a sense of vertigo; that is, technology has moved faster than our understanding of its implications. To pretend any educator or institution has the singular, right approach to the ever-evolving AI availability is disingenuous. The approach does not exist, and we have been figuring out that our early efforts to combat students’ unethical AI use are falling short. The surveillance tactics and fear-messaging have not curbed AI use. We know checkers can be faulty, and trust between teachers and students has been negatively impacted (Luo).

It is easy to understand how the varied responses to AI across institutions, society, and classrooms have left students feeling confused, causing many to stay silent while attempting to discern how much AI use, if any, crosses the line.

For example, this past May, commencement speakers at multiple graduation ceremonies were booed for their references to AI. This includes a business executive who was booed by arts and humanities graduates after referring to the rise of AI as “the next industrial revolution” (Shahin).

All students deserve a voice in discussions about AI, including those who question its larger implications and those who embrace its potential as a learning tool. Students are navigating the same often conflicting landscape as teachers and higher ed administrators. With more student participation in these conversations, perhaps we can turn the page from reactive responses to proactive engagement.

My own students, along with those whose voices we hear at commencements and across digital platforms, offer a collective reminder: few groups have as much at stake in the future of AI as Generation Z, and from their front row seat, they see that in higher education, approaches to AI run the gamut – from signed “I will not use AI” contracts and blue-book essays to “cite your use of AI.”

Teachers also observe the wide range of responses in higher education. The last few years, most conversations with my English colleagues have involved our efforts to try to AI-proof our online writing classes – with emphasis on the word try. As AI becomes more pervasive, we are all grappling with the same core questions: How do we protect human creativity, judgment, and connection? How do we continue to make learning meaningful? As my student reminded me, students are in college for a reason.

For me, as I have (more or less) left behind the use of AI checkers, I’m ready for less AI surveillance. I prefer to use that energy for increased dialogue with my students about what learning requires. I am ready for more two-sided conversations, student reflection, and shared inquiry into what represents true learning. And I will continue to encourage students to own their own writing and to emphasize how – in their written compositions – their voice makes the difference.

Trust Between Students and Teachers

Over the last few years, I have attended multiple professional development meetings tied to AI literacy. Few included students’ comments. My own student’s observation (“I’m in college for a reason”) made me consider my own voice and how relaxed I have become with waiting for direction from higher ups.

Math teacher Al Rabanera writes about a similar wake-up call: “I didn’t realize how much agency I had lost as a California teacher until AI showed me what I’d been missing.” Rabanera said AI revealed “how comfortable [he had] become with waiting. Waiting for district guidance. . . . Waiting to be told not just what to do, but how to think.”

As this past academic year concluded, one other reflection lingered with me: A heavy emphasis on warnings about AI use, followed by detection and required meetings with students who submitted AI-written drafts, particularly in my online non-synchronous classes, tainted the spirit of the classes. As Matthew Brophy points out, “When pedagogy tilts toward detection over development, it cultivates a classroom ethos of suspicion rather than community.”

Jess Luo explains, ”Trusting relationships between teachers and students are crucial in developing effective teaching, learning and assessment,” and “there is discernible concern among the higher education community that GenAI is causing an ‘erosion of trust’ between students and their teachers.”

Below are strategies to reset the table and to turn the focus of classes in the age of AI from “accusatory ambience [that] breeds anxiety” (Brophy) to purposeful, fun engagement.

Beginning-of-the-Semester Reflection

Ask students to reflect on their educational and career goals; to reflect on what they will learn in the course and the skills they will obtain. What challenges do they anticipate? What are strategies to offset those obstacles? In sum, their reflection of goals should reinforce for them why it is meaningful to be in college.

This early reflection aligns with what Pauline Stamp refers to as “Purpose-First Learning.” She suggests that teachers start day one by inviting students “to engage each learning objective [of the course]” and answer questions like “What does this objective mean to you? Why does it matter—personally, professionally, or socially?” Stamp points out that “engagement . . . emerges when learners understand why the learning matters to them.”

Ask students to reflect on their AI use – both in their private lives and in academia. Use reflection survey results to generate discussion about AI – the ways it is used in our personal lives, the mixed messaging that surrounds it, and the ethical/non-ethical use of it in college classes. This discussion needs to be a dialogue.

Student reflections, individual and collective, open the door for more conversations. When students are engaged, when they can see the value of the work, they are more likely to sit with an assignment, to analyze a prompt closely, and to seize ownership of their writing. Conversely, a Swansea University study concludes that “disengaged students are more likely to use AI tools—particularly ChatGPT—for academic assignments.”

Other strategies to build trust and investment in a class are not new and long predate the heavy AI influx:

Along with increased dialogue, provide students with clear guidance on each assignment.

Return students’ work quickly.

Facilitate opportunities for students to reflect on their own growth in the course.

When possible, comment on work in stages.

Provide individualized feedback to students; look for opportunities to point them toward paper topics and/or experiential learning opportunities that are likely to be of interest.

From my vantage point, as some of the smoke begins to clear in the AI-infused era, what has been missing are student voices. Students are living with the realities of AI every day. They deserve a genuine seat at the table in discussions about learning and technology. Meaningful learning depends on classrooms built on trust, dialogue, and shared reflection rather than fear or suspicion. The adage still rings true: We learn as much from our students as they do from us. My student this past spring inspired me not only to remember that students are in college for a reason but also to recall my own agency as a teacher and to encourage students to harness their own voices.

Dr. Mary Ruth Wallen brings over three decades of college teaching experience to her work. A native of Inez, Kentucky, she holds dual B.A. degrees in English and Journalism from Morehead State University (1995), an M.A. in English with a creative writing emphasis from Indiana State University (1997), an MFA in Fiction from Southern Illinois University–Carbondale (2003), and a Doctorate of Arts in English Pedagogy from Murray State University (2021). Since 2003, she has been teaching at Big Sandy Community and Technical College in Prestonsburg, KY. Dr. Wallen believes that strong writing transcends genre and empowers all who practice it.

title: 5 Lessons for Building Institutional AI Capacity in Resource Constrained Settings
summary:
Higher education institutions face growing pressure to respond to generative artificial intelligence. At Cochise College in rural southeastern Arizona, a four-year, $1.87 million federal grant, AI-Powered Success, is helping us take a community empowerment approach to building AI literacy across the institution and region. A foundational/scalable framework informs professional development for faculty; institutional capacity-building for staff, K–12 and industry partnerships; and workforce microcredentials with stackable badges tied to college credit.
Along the way, we have learned five…
full_text:
1. Start With Readiness, Not Tools

Before investing in platforms or training, find out what people need to understand and what would help them feel psychologically prepared to experiment. We started with listening sessions, faculty brainstorming activities and low-risk experimentation opportunities. These helped surface concerns and build psychological safety. AI does not act on everyone equally because it amplifies both existing skills as well as deficits that people bring to it.

Our initial needs analysis revealed that the biggest barriers to AI adoption were not technical. People expressed uncertainty about ethical use, accuracy, student misuse and their own knowledge. Few were asking which tools to buy.

2. Teach Judgment, Not Just Rules

Many institutions approach AI with policies rather than heuristics. These tend to boil AI use down to what is allowed, limited or prohibited. Our foundational/scalable framework focuses on equipping human professional judgment and growing user confidence in AI decision-making. It guides people to develop a habitual mindset of asking when, why and how AI inputs and outputs are useful to particular tasks.

Foundational skills are those learners need to develop rather than bypass with AI. Scalable skills are those AI can extend or amplify. Without foundational AI skills, scaling is not possible and policies serve only to blindly limit confidence and experimentation. For IT leaders, increasing foundational capacity complements security policies and acceptable-use guidelines by developing the human judgment needed to recognize risks, evaluate outputs and make informed decisions for long-term scalability and sustainability.

DISCOVER: Higher ed institutions are adopting a human-centered approach to technology.

3. Invest in People Before Platforms

Recognizing that AI is an equity issue is crucial to the success of our programming. AI literacy is becoming a condition of employment. We decided early and adamantly to invest in people. Thus, we are spending money on capacity building, not technology purchases. Tools change; the capacity stays. We made sure the project could touch everyone in the college, our community, and beyond. We are also approaching each initiative one at a time, per grant year, instead of launching all of them at once. This helps ensure each has the capacity to succeed before the next begins. Eventually, all of this documentation will end up in an open educational resource library, making it accessible to other institutions.

4. Design for the Range, not the Average

Our AI Innovation Studio brought together faculty and staff with widely varying experience and opinions. We trained everyone from complete beginners to advanced users already building their own bots. Some had enthusiastically adopted AI early without the necessary critical examination or boundaries, while others sought to disprove the use of AI altogether.

The curriculum that brings this to center is based on a triangulation protocol. The first leg is to raise ethical questions for the context in which AI is being proposed for use. Should I use AI? The second is to scan for security risks pertinent to the information one is entering into the AI tool. How should I safeguard data? Last, outputs are put through a trust lab that structures critical thinking about the applicability and veracity of what AI produces. Is the AI output reliable? This protocol is woven into every training level and product.

Den wenigstens Studierenden fällt es einfach, ein Thema für eine wissenschaftliche Abschlussarbeit zu finden. Man muss nicht nur ein Thema festlegen, sondern dieses auch eingrenzen, eine passende Fragestellung dazu formulieren und sich dann überlegen, wo man mit der Recherche beginnt. Hilfreich ist es, wenn man bei all dem einen Dialogpartner hat, mit dem man seine Ideen diskutieren kann. In diesem Blogbeitrag zeigen Melanie Dejnega und Evelyn Fränzl, dass dieser Dialogpartner auch ein Chatbot sein kann.

Ein tragfähiges Thema ist eine wichtige Voraussetzung für eine gelingende Abschlussarbeit – und oft eine der ersten großen Hürden. Gerade in dieser Phase brauchen Studierende Rückmeldung: Ist die Idee noch zu breit? Lässt sie sich sinnvoll eingrenzen? Und wonach sollten sie eigentlich recherchieren?

In mehreren unserer Bachelorstudiengänge an der FHWien der WKW findet diese Themenentwicklung zu einem Zeitpunkt statt, an dem die Studierenden noch ohne Betreuungsverhältnis sind und ihr Bedarf an individuellem Feedback im Rahmen von Lehrveranstaltungen nicht hinreichend gedeckt werden kann.

Genau hier haben wir im Rahmen des von der MA23 der Stadt Wien geförderten Projekts „Master Propaedeutics – Brückenkurse wissenschaftliches Arbeiten“ angesetzt und „Donna, den Themenbuddy“ entwickelt: ein Custom GPT (basierend auf ChatGPT), das Studierende bei der Themenentwicklung unterstützt. Allerdings mit einer wichtigen Einschränkung: Donna soll die Studierenden durch systematisches Nachfragen bei der eigenständigen Problemlösung begleiten, anstatt ihnen fertige Lösungen zu präsentieren.

Unsere Erfahrungen aus zwei Lehrveranstaltungsdurchläufen zeigen: Der didaktische Wert solcher KI-Tutor:innen liegt nicht darin, Studierenden fachliche Entscheidungen abzunehmen. Sinnvoll werden sie dort, wo sie zusätzliche Räume zum Nachdenken schaffen.

Die Idee ist nicht neu. Katharina Opper stellte bereits 2023 im HFD-Blog die Frage, wie sich generative KI nicht als Lieferantin fertiger Antworten, sondern als Impulsgeberin für kritisches Denken einsetzen lässt (Opper, 2023). Daran haben wir angeknüpft. Erfahrungen mit KI-gestützten Tutor:innen in studentischen Forschungsprozessen haben wir bereits in einem früheren Beitrag beschrieben (Neuburger et al., 2025).

Menschliche wie KI-gestützte Tutor:innen, die sich am Prinzip des sokratischen Dialogs orientieren, geben nicht vorschnell Lösungen vor. Stattdessen regen sie Studierende mit offenen Fragen dazu an, eigene Überlegungen zu entwickeln und zu hinterfragen (Fakour & Imani, 2025; Favero et al., 2025). Antworten und Schlussfolgerungen sollen dabei von den Studierenden selbst kommen.

Studien deuten darauf hin, dass diese Form des „Denktrainings“ die eigenständige Auseinandersetzung mit einem Thema, die Argumentation und den kritischen Blick auf unterschiedliche Perspektiven unterstützen können (siehe z. B. Bui & Nguyen, 2026; Santos-Guevara et al., 2026).

Wir haben Donna in zwei Lehrveranstaltungsdurchläufen eingesetzt. Die Wahrnehmung der Studierenden haben wir sowohl in Gesprächen während der Lehrveranstaltungen als auch mit einer standardisierten Befragung erhoben.

Das unmittelbare Feedback war überwiegend positiv. Viele Studierende wollten Donna auch nach Abschluss der Lehrveranstaltung weiterverwenden. Gleichzeitig wurden klare Grenzen sichtbar. Einige hätten in dieser Phase lieber mit einer realen Lehrperson gesprochen. Mehrfach wurde betont, dass der KI-gestützte Dialog ein Gespräch mit Lehrenden oder späteren Betreuer:innen nicht ersetzen sollte.

Auch technische Rahmenbedingungen spielten eine Rolle. Bei Studierenden ohne kostenpflichtigen ChatGPT-Zugang führten Nutzungslimits teilweise dazu, dass sie den Dialog mit Donna auf mehrere Tage verteilen mussten. Das klingt zunächst nach einem Nebenaspekt, ist für die didaktische Planung aber relevant: Ein Lernangebot ist nur dann niedrigschwellig, wenn es auch tatsächlich für alle Studierenden zugänglich ist.

Als besonders interessant stellten sich die Ergebnisse der standardisierten Befragung zu Semesterende heraus. Insgesamt beantworteten 69 Studierende Fragen zu ihrer Wahrnehmung von Donna.

Auf einer siebenstufigen Skala bewerteten die Studierenden die Kommunikation mit Donna insgesamt positiv (M = 4,99; SD = 0,94). Besonders hoch fielen die Bewertungen für die wahrgenommene Kompetenz (M = 5,22; SD = 0,98) aus. Etwas geringer fielen die Bewertungen von Donnas fachlicher Expertise (M = 4,86; SD = 1,19) sowie das Vertrauen der Studierenden in ihre Kompetenz (M = 4,75; SD = 1,19) aus. Ein gepaarter t-Test zeigte einen statistisch signifikanten Unterschied: Donna wurde als kompetenter wahrgenommen, als ihr tatsächlich vertraut wurde (p < 0,001; d = 0,50). Die Ergebnisse legen nahe, dass die wahrgenommene Kompetenz Donnas nicht zwangsläufig mit Vertrauen in ebendiese einhergeht. Und das ist für diesen Anwendungsfall durchaus wünschenswert.

Donna soll Ideen hinterfragen, zur Präzisierung auffordern und weitere Überlegungen anstoßen. Doch auch gut konfigurierte KI-Tutor:innen können problematische Annahmen bestätigen, fachliche Besonderheiten übersehen oder zu einer Eingrenzung führen, die auf den ersten Blick plausibel wirkt, sich bei der Literaturrecherche aber nicht trägt.

Deshalb braucht der sokratische KI-Dialog aus unserer Sicht einen klaren nächsten Schritt: Auf die KI-gestützte Reflexion müssen eine fundierte Auseinandersetzung mit dem Thema sowie die fachliche Einordnung und Rückmeldung durch Lehrende folgen – etwa im Rahmen von Lehrveranstaltungen, Betreuungssettings oder anderen fachlichen Austauschformaten.

Die KI-Tutor:innen stehen damit nicht am Ende des Themenfindungsprozesses, sondern am Anfang.

Unsere Befragung erfasst Wahrnehmungen, keine Lernzuwächse. Wir können daher nicht sagen, ob Studierende mit Donna objektiv bessere Bachelorarbeitsthemen entwickelt haben. Ebenso wenig wissen wir bislang, ob sich der Dialog auf die Qualität der späteren Arbeiten auswirkt.

Spannend wären deshalb weitere Untersuchungen, die Themenstände vor und nach dem KI-Dialog vergleichen, Gesprächsverläufe analysieren oder untersuchen, welche Arten von Rückfragen tatsächlich zu einer stärkeren Präzisierung führen.

Für die Praxis lässt sich dennoch eine Schlussfolgerung ziehen: Sokratische KI-Tutor:innen können zusätzliche individuelle Reflexionsgelegenheiten schaffen, wenn ihre Aufgabe klar begrenzt und ihr Einsatz didaktisch eingebettet ist. Auf diesem Weg können sie Reflexions- und Problemlösungsprozesse unterstützen. Die Verantwortung für fachliche Einordnung, Rückmeldung und Betreuung muss aber bei den Lehrenden bleiben. Gerade diese Arbeitsteilung macht die KI-Chatbots, die auf dem Prinzip des sokratischen Dialogs basieren, für die Hochschullehre besonders interessant.
